source.title: A Sharper Picture of Generalization in Transformers

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including supplementary material; some figure values are not available as text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization and sharpness on synthetic Boolean-function tasks using transformer models, rather than the claim versions’ natural-label benchmarks and specific interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper studies real-valued targets on Boolean inputs, not natural labels or random-label memorization. It reports empirical generalization-gap and Hessian-trace results relevant to sharpness, but does not test the magnitude-aware perturbation measure specified in V7. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study reports generalization gaps and Hessian-trace sharpness for transformers learning synthetic functions. These results concern a different construct from V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and do not test any other listed version. Its batch-size observation concerns convergence, without a fixed-epoch comparison of held-out performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors construct transformers with bounded norm and Hessian-trace sharpness for restricted Fourier-function classes and derive conditional PAC-Bayes guarantees for perturbed predictors under an explicit joint norm-and-sharpness domination assumption. Empirically, gaps increase with degree and sparsity, and learned solutions have lower norm and Hessian trace than the construction. Practical non-vacuous bounds use an empirically estimated perturbation term; the fully analytic bound is much looser. Mechanistic similarities are illustrative and close matches are rare.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic Boolean-domain function learning with transformer models; uses Hessian trace and a theoretical PAC-Bayes construction rather than the claim versions’ natural-label experiments or magnitude-aware perturbation measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The empirical generalization gap varies with target-function degree and Fourier sparsity. Batch size affects convergence likelihood; degree-5 functions were difficult to learn above batch size 256. Adding or removing layer normalization did not qualitatively change results.

fits_no_version.finding: Among successfully trained target functions, empirical generalization gaps rise super-linearly with Fourier degree, with a steeper increase at greater sparsity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested transformer and selected convergent Boolean-domain regression tasks, generalization gaps increase with target-function degree and sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned solutions have training-loss Hessian traces roughly two orders of magnitude below the explicit construction across the tested degree and sparsity classes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned transformers can implement the tested functions with substantially lower Hessian-trace sharpness than this explicit construction.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A reports difficulty learning degree-5 functions with batch sizes above 256, without a held-out-performance comparison at matched epoch budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size affects convergence on the tested high-degree synthetic function-learning tasks.

record.problems: The main learner assumption is an oracle-style domination assumption, supported empirically only in the tested regime. Main generalization-gap experiments use real-valued targets on Boolean inputs and a deliberately larger model; the theoretical construction assumes positive Fourier coefficients, constant component degree, and sparsity ω ≤ T. The paper says close mechanistic matches are rare. Some relevant values are only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No numeric figure values were recoverable from the text, so plotted values are recorded as figure only. Cited results from earlier studies, including optimizer, batch-size, architecture, dropout, and sharpness comparisons, are excluded.

untested.parts: Matched random-label fitting and natural-label generalization, including chance-level held-out performance on random labels.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of learned local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance under specified tuning budgets.
Large-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce its penalty.
Controlled dropout comparisons, training-set-size effects, and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps among comparably fitted networks, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Neither isotropic perturbations of the explicit construction nor Hessian-trace measurements supply this test.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The theoretical low-sharpness learner is an assumption, not evidence for V7. Row states indicate inability to determine a listed version's effect, rather than disputing the paper's descriptive findings. No omitted result directly bearing on V1–V8 was identified.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects and interaction with augmentation or weight decay.
The study measures Hessian-trace sharpness, not magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, and does not rank that measure against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: simple transformer with 2 layers and 1 head
rows.operation_detail: Measured empirical generalization gap across sparse Fourier–Walsh target-function classes.
rows.uncertainty: figure shows average over a sample of 11 functions from each Degree, Sparsity class; no numeric uncertainty stated in text
rows.note: Authors state the gap increases super-linearly with degree, and its rate of increase increases with larger sparsity. Figure values are not transcribed. Appendix A gives a different function-sampling count; this row follows the Figure 1 description.
rows.check: The reported degree-and-sparsity trend is supported descriptively but measures no listed version. Appendix A says some nonconvergent degree-5 targets were replaced, so the results concern selected convergent functions. The paper inconsistently reports 5 versus 11 functions per class; Figure 1 and the later implementation description specify 11.

rows.subject: learned solutions from the simple transformer with 2 layers and 1 head
rows.stage_stated: trained solutions; exact training loss not stated for this comparison
rows.operation_detail: Measured trace of the training-loss Hessian for learned solutions across degree and sparsity classes.

conditions.value: 11 randomly generated functions per degree and sparsity class

rows.note: The figure compares learned solutions with the exact construction; the text says construction sharpness is higher by roughly two orders of magnitude. The text also notes the degree-5 increase is less steep than expected relative to the construction. No per-class numerical values are stated.
rows.check: Hessian trace is not V7's magnitude-aware perturbation-tolerance measure. The roughly hundredfold difference compares learned solutions with the authors' explicit construction; it does not establish that sharpness ranks generalization gaps. Figure 2 identifies these as the same trained models used in Figure 1, so Appendix A's training-loss threshold below 0.02 applies.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
